slides.title: Saying no
slides.text:
Negative words say **no**.

**not**, **no**, **never**

I am **not** sleepy. I have **no** pen.

slides.title: Short forms
slides.text:
do not → **don't**
cannot → **can't**
is not → **isn't**

The **'** shows where letters are missing.

slides.title: One is enough
slides.text:
Use **one** no-word for one idea.

✓ I don't have a pen.
✗ I don't have no pen.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Point to the no-words in the sentence: not, n't, no, never.
2. Count them.
3. More than one for the same idea? That is a mistake.

sentences.t: I never play outside when it rains.

example.explain:
**don't** and **never** are no-words. Each sentence has only **one**.

"I like the sun" has no no-word.

together.passage: Sami looked for his ball. He did not find it. He said, "I can't see it anywhere." Then he saw it under the bed.
together.stem: Which word in the text is the short form of cannot?
together.hint: Look for a word with an ' in it.
together.good: Yes! Can't is the short form of cannot. The ' shows where letters are missing.

sentences: Sami looked for his ball.
He did not find it.
He said, "I can't see it anywhere."
Then he saw it under the bed.
evidence.stem: Tap 2 sentences that have a no-word.
evidence.wrong: This sentence has no no-word. Look for not or n't.

checks.why: We say I don't like spiders. It has one no-word.
Doesn't and no are both no-words. Use one: Omar doesn't have any lunch, or Omar has no lunch.
Never is a no-word. It means not at any time.

again.title: Count to one
again.text:
Find the no-words. Count them.

**One** → good!
**Two** → take one out.
again.example:
I don't want no juice.

No-words: **don't**, **no**. That is two! → I don't want **any** juice.

slides.title: Double negatives
slides.text:
Two no-words for one idea make a **double negative**.

✗ I don't want nothing.

In correct English, use only **one**.

slides.title: Two ways to fix it
slides.text:
1. Keep **not**, change the other word: I don't want **anything**.
2. Drop **not**, keep the no-word: I want **nothing**.

slides.title: Partners
slides.text:
nothing ↔ anything
nobody ↔ anybody
nowhere ↔ anywhere
never ↔ ever
no ↔ any

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Point to every no-word: not, n't, no, never, nothing, nobody, nowhere.
2. Two of them for one idea? That sentence has the mistake.
3. Point to it, then fix it with an **any** word.

sentences.t: We didn't see anybody at the park.
There was nobody on the swings.

example.explain:
Sentence 1: **didn't** + **anybody**. One no-word.

Sentence 2: **nobody** alone. One no-word.

Both say the same thing correctly.

together.passage: My brother Khalid is a picky eater. At dinner, he said, "I don't want no vegetables." Mom smiled and put a small plate of carrots in front of him. Khalid tried one. "These aren't bad at all," he said. Soon there was nothing left on his plate.
together.stem: Which sentence has a double negative?
options: My brother Khalid is a picky eater.
At dinner, he said, "I don't want no vegetables."
"These aren't bad at all," he said.
Soon there was nothing left on his plate.
together.hint: Count the no-words in each sentence. Which one has two for the same idea?
together.good: Yes! Don't and no are two no-words. It should be: I don't want any vegetables.

sentences: My brother Khalid is a picky eater.
At dinner, he said, "I don't want no vegetables."
Mom smiled and put a small plate of carrots in front of him.
Khalid tried one.
"These aren't bad at all," he said.
Soon there was nothing left on his plate.
evidence.stem: Tap 2 sentences that use one no-word correctly.
evidence.wrong: This sentence has no no-word at all, or it has two. Find sentences with exactly one.

checks.passage: I can't find my shoes nowhere.
options: I can't find no shoes nowhere.
I can find my shoes nowhere not.
I can't not find my shoes.
I can't find my shoes anywhere.
checks.why: Can't is the one no-word, so nowhere changes to its partner anywhere.
Nobody is already a no-word, so we use has, not hasn't.

checks.passage: We didn't buy ___ at the market.
checks.why: Didn't is the no-word, so we use the partner anything.

again.title: Swap for any
again.text:
Already have **not** or **n't**? Swap the other no-word for its **any** partner.

nothing → anything
nobody → anybody
nowhere → anywhere
again.example:
She didn't tell nobody.

Keep **didn't**. Swap **nobody** → **anybody**.

**She didn't tell anybody.**

slides.title: More negative words
slides.text:
**nobody / no one**, **nothing**, **nowhere**, **none**, **neither**, **never**

Each one already means **no**. Do not add another negative.

slides.title: The hidden not
slides.text:
The **n't** in don't, can't, won't, isn't is a negative too.

✗ She isn't never late.
✓ She is never late.
✓ She isn't ever late.

slides.title: Neither ... nor
slides.text:
**Neither ... nor** means not this one and not that one.

**Neither** Ali **nor** Sami was absent.

✗ Neither Ali nor Sami wasn't absent.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the part of the sentence that says no.
2. Count every negative in it, including **n't**.
3. Point to the extra one. That is the proof of the mistake.

sentences.t: Neither my sister nor I have ever been to Jeddah.
We hope to go there someday.

example.explain:
**Neither ... nor** is the only negative. It is paired with **ever**, not never.

One negative idea, one negative.

together.passage: Dear Grandma, thank you for the beautiful scarf. Nobody in my class has ever had one like it! The weather here isn't never cold, but I wear it on windy evenings. My brother says he doesn't want a scarf, but I think he wishes he had one. Neither of us has forgotten your visit last spring.
together.stem: Which sentence needs to be fixed?
options: Nobody in my class has ever had one like it!
The weather here isn't never cold, but I wear it on windy evenings.
My brother says he doesn't want a scarf.
Neither of us has forgotten your visit last spring.
together.hint: Count the negatives in each idea. Remember that n't counts!
together.good: Yes! Isn't and never are two negatives. It should be: The weather here is never cold.

sentences: Dear Grandma, thank you for the beautiful scarf.
Nobody in my class has ever had one like it!
The weather here isn't never cold, but I wear it on windy evenings.
My brother says he doesn't want a scarf, but I think he wishes he had one.
Neither of us has forgotten your visit last spring.
evidence.stem: Tap 2 sentences that use only one negative correctly.
evidence.wrong: This sentence has no negative, or it has two for one idea.

checks.why: Isn't is the one negative, so none changes to any.

checks.passage: Neither the bus nor the train ___ on time today.
checks.why: Neither ... nor is already negative, so we use was, not wasn't.

checks.passage: I have never seen nothing like it!
options: I have never seen anything like it!
I haven't never seen anything like it!
I have never not seen nothing like it!
I have ever seen nothing like it!
checks.why: Never is the one negative, so nothing changes to anything.

again.title: Circle the negatives
again.text:
Circle every **no**, **not**, **n't**, **never** and **no-** word.

Two circles in one idea? Remove one, or swap it for an **any** / **ever** word.
again.example:
Nobody never helps me.

Circles: **Nobody**, **never**. → **Nobody ever helps me.**

slides.title: Hidden negative words
slides.text:
**hardly**, **barely** and **scarcely** already mean almost **not**.

✗ I can't hardly hear you.
✓ I can hardly hear you.

**without** works the same way: ✗ He left without saying nothing. ✓ He left without saying **anything**.

slides.title: Two negatives on purpose
slides.text:
Sometimes writers put **not** before a word with a negative **prefix**: not **un**usual, not **im**possible.

The two cancel out and make a softer **positive**.

It is not unusual = it is fairly common.

slides.title: Formal writing
slides.text:
In everyday speech, some people use double negatives.

In school and formal writing, use **one negative per idea**, unless you mean a softened positive like not unkind.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Point to every negative in the clause: not, n't, no-words, hardly, barely, scarcely, without.
2. Two in one idea → revise it.
3. A not + un- or im- pair → work out the positive meaning it makes.

sentences.t: The trail was steep, and we could barely see the path in the fog.
Still, it was not impossible to reach the top.

example.explain:
**could barely see**: barely is the only negative, so it is correct.

**not impossible**: two negatives on purpose. It means it **was possible**, though hard.

together.passage: The winter storm in the northern region lasted three days. Roads were closed, and some villages had barely any electricity. Hardly anyone left their homes. On the second night, a group of volunteers drove through the snow without stopping for nothing, delivering blankets and food to older neighbors. For people in the area, snow in winter is not unusual, but a storm this strong is rare. By the fourth day, the roads had reopened, and nobody had been seriously hurt.
together.stem: Which phrase should be revised for formal writing?
together.hint: Without is a hidden negative. Is there another negative in the same idea?
together.good: Yes! Without and nothing are two negatives for one idea. It should be: without stopping for anything.

sentences: The winter storm in the northern region lasted three days.
Roads were closed, and some villages had barely any electricity.
Hardly anyone left their homes.
On the second night, a group of volunteers drove through the snow without stopping for nothing, delivering blankets and food to older neighbors.
For people in the area, snow in winter is not unusual, but a storm this strong is rare.
By the fourth day, the roads had reopened, and nobody had been seriously hurt.
evidence.stem: Tap 2 sentences that use a hidden negative (barely or hardly) correctly.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not use barely or hardly correctly. Look for a hidden negative paired with an any word.

checks.passage: The room was so dark that I couldn't barely see.
options: The room was so dark that I couldn't hardly see.
The room was so dark that I could not see barely nothing.
The room was so dark that I could barely see.
The room was so dark that I couldn't barely not see.
checks.why: Barely is already a negative, so n't must go: I could barely see.

checks.passage: Finishing the project in one day is not impossible.
checks.stem: What does not impossible mean here?
options: It can be done, though it may be hard.
checks.why: Not and im- cancel out, making a softer positive: it is possible, but not easy.

checks.passage: He left the meeting without saying ___ to anyone.
checks.why: Without is a hidden negative, so we use the partner anything.

again.title: Spot the hidden ones
again.text:
Some negatives hide: **hardly**, **barely**, **scarcely**, **without**.

Treat them like **not**. Pair them with **any**, **ever** or **anyone**, never with another no-word.
again.example:
We hardly saw nobody.

**hardly** is a negative already → **We hardly saw anybody.**
